readingInstruction: Read Micah 1:1-3:12. Micah was a prophet from a small town in Judah, and he speaks for the poor against the powerful. Read these chapters as a courtroom speech, and notice who is accused.
settingTheScene: Micah prophesied in Judah during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, in the same period as Isaiah and Hosea. He came from Moresheth, a village in the countryside, far from the court. His message is about both Samaria and Jerusalem. Where Hosea spoke of love, and Amos of justice, Micah brings both together and ends with a promise of a ruler from Bethlehem.
observation: “Hear, you peoples, all of you; pay attention, O earth, and all that is in it, and let the Lord GOD be a witness against you” (1:2).
“Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand” (2:1).
“They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, a man and his inheritance” (2:2).
“If a man should go about and utter wind and lies, saying, I will preach to you of wine and strong drink, he would be the preacher for this people!” (2:11).
“Is it not for you to know justice?” (3:1).
“You who hate the good and love the evil, who tear the skin from off my people” (3:2).
“Its heads give judgment for a bribe; its priests teach for a price; its prophets practice divination for money” (3:11).
“But as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD, and with justice and might, to declare to Jacob his transgression and to Israel his sin” (3:8).
interpretation:
Micah begins with a cosmic summons. All the peoples of the earth are called to hear, and the LORD himself comes down from his temple, the mountains melt under his feet. The first judgment falls on Samaria and Judah for idolatry and corruption. The prophet is so grieved that he goes barefoot and naked and wails like a jackal.

The center of chapter 2 is economic sin. People lie awake at night planning how to seize fields and houses. Because they have the power, they do it. This is not a distant, abstract evil. It is landowners taking the inheritance of poorer families, each one of whom held land as a gift of the covenant. To take the land is to attack God’s gift. And Micah notes that the people prefer false prophets: if a man preaches comfort, wine, and strong drink, he is their kind of preacher.

Chapter 3 turns on the leaders. Rulers who should know justice hate the good. Micah uses a shocking image: they eat the flesh of the people and flay their skin. When they cry to the LORD, he will not answer. Prophets who mislead the people for money will find that the vision becomes night. Then Micah gives his own claim: “I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the LORD.” His message is not his own invention. It has the authority of God’s Spirit.

The chapter ends with a verdict: “Therefore because of you Zion shall be plowed as a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of ruins.” Jeremiah 26:18 later recalls that this prophecy saved Jerusalem in Hezekiah’s day, because the king listened and repented. Hard words can lead to healing when they are heard.

Yet in the middle of chapter 2, there is a flicker of hope: “I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob… I will set them together like sheep in a fold.” The LORD will be the king who breaks open the way and leads his people out. Judgment is not the last word.
connection: Jesus announced the good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and warned against those who devour widows’ houses (Mark 12:40). James 5:1-6 warns the rich who defraud workers. Acts 1:8 promises power from the Holy Spirit to witness, as Micah was filled with the Spirit to declare. 1 Peter 5:2-3 charges elders to shepherd the flock willingly, not for shameful gain.
application:
Ask whether any of your gain comes at someone else’s expense. Look closely at your work and spending.

Pray for leaders in the church to teach faithfully and not for a price.

Pray for the courage to speak truth, as Micah did, in the power of the Spirit.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from coveting and seizing what is not yours.
Pray for church leaders to be faithful and free from greed.
Ask him to fill you with power, justice, and might by his Spirit.
